vignette:
When Dara was first stalked, it began in the ordinary spaces of his working life. At 50, a divorced Cambodian American musician, he was used to late nights loading equipment after sets, greeting strangers after performances, and moving between bars, rehearsal rooms, and small venues across the city. The man first appeared after a show, standing too long near the stage door, then outside Dara's apartment building, then again at a grocery store several neighborhoods away. Over the next weeks the encounters took on a terrible pattern: repeated messages from unknown numbers, gifts left where he would find them, footsteps behind him after midnight when he carried his instrument case to his car. One night, after a performance, Dara saw the man waiting across the street under a flickering light, not approaching, just watching. Dara remembered hurrying to unlock his car while hearing his own breathing and the scrape of shoes on pavement behind him. After that night, parts of what happened blurred. He could recall the glare of the streetlight on the windshield, the smell of stale beer from the alley, and the sensation that someone was close enough to touch him, but there were stretches he simply could not retrieve no matter how hard he tried.

What hardened the experience into something ongoing was not only the stalking itself but Dara's conviction that no one who should have protected him really did. He reported the incidents and felt brushed off, as if repeated surveillance and unwanted contact did not count until something worse happened. He had come to believe that institutions had failed him, and that belief quickly became personal: if he could not stop this, if he kept freezing and second-guessing himself, then maybe he was a weak person. From there, his world narrowed. He began avoiding unfamiliar places because he felt he could not judge danger there, and at gigs in new venues he would scan exits, doorways, and the faces in the crowd instead of settling into the music. At night, especially after performances, he found it much harder to feel safe at all. He watched other people closely for signs that they might harm him, certain that letting his guard down would mean missing the next threat.

Those same beliefs also shaped the way the stalking lived in his mind. When he tried to remember clearly, the missing pieces seemed to confirm his sense that he had failed in some basic way; he told himself a stronger man would know exactly what happened and what to do about it. His anger that nobody had stepped in left him going back over the worst moments, but not in a coherent story. Instead the memory returned in sudden shards: the glow of a phone screen in the dark, footsteps matching his pace, a figure across the street. At other times it hit with full force, as though the event were happening again in the present, complete across sight, sound, and body sensation. The vividness frightened him, but the gaps frightened him too, because both seemed like proof that the experience had gotten inside him and changed him.

As the months passed, the memory itself began to organize his days. A stranger lingering too long near a club entrance or someone walking behind him after a set could bring back the sensory reliving at once, and once that happened Dara became even more vigilant. He monitored every face, every movement of a hand into a pocket, every pause outside a backstage door. He stopped accepting bookings in unfamiliar neighborhoods and would only agree to play in venues he knew well, often asking staff to walk him to his car. These habits cost him work. Other musicians noticed he was distracted and rigid, more preoccupied with the room than with rehearsal, and he turned down collaborative opportunities if they involved new spaces or late-night travel.

The cycle tightened further because his vigilance kept the stalking present. Nights were the worst: lying awake listening for sounds in the hallway, he would catch a fragment of memory without warning, and his body would react as though the man were outside again. Watching other people so closely during the day left him keyed up and exhausted, and in that strained state the old scenes broke through more easily and more vividly. Each time this happened, Dara felt more dead inside afterward. He described an emptiness that was almost worse than fear, as if he had gone numb in order to keep functioning. That numbness fed his belief that something essential in him had been damaged, and when he saw himself as weakened and unprotected, he became even less able to relax his guard.

By the time he sought help, Dara's life had constricted to a small circuit of familiar venues, daytime errands, and careful routes home. He still played music, but the pleasure had thinned; he spent performances studying the audience for danger and nights listening for pursuit. What finally brought him in was a recent episode after a show when a man in the parking lot glanced at him twice and Dara was suddenly back under that streetlight, heart pounding, senses flooded, unable to tell how much of what he was seeing belonged to now and how much belonged to then. He said he was tired of living as if threat were always one step behind him, but what frightened him most was the possibility that he was right to stay this alert-that if he stopped watching, no one would protect him, and the next time he might not get away.
